8: NVIDIA Announces Financial Results for Third Quarter Fiscal 2027
9: •Revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year ago
10: •Data Center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year ago
11: •Vera Rubin NVL72, the most versatile and advanced computing platform ever built, has shipped
12: SANTA CLARA, Calif.—Nov. 17, 2026―NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today reported revenue for the third quarter ended October 25, 2026, of $115.8 billion, up 20% from the previous quarter and up 103% from a year ago. For the quarter, GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins were 74.8% and 74.9%, respectively. GAAP and non-GAAP earnings per diluted share were $2.70 and $2.68, respectively.
13: “Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” said Colette Kress, interim CEO and executive vice president and chief financial officer of NVIDIA. “Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.”
14: In September 2026, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors approved an increase of $150 billion to the company’s share repurchase authorization, without expiration. During the third quarter of fiscal 2027, NVIDIA returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the form of shares repurchased and cash dividends. As of the end of the third quarter, the company had approximately $227.3 billion remaining under its share repurchase authorization.
15: NVIDIA will pay its next quarterly cash dividend of $0.25 per share on December 23, 2026, to all shareholders of record on December 2, 2026.

35: Outlook
36: NVIDIA’s outlook for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, which includes an additional week, is as follows:
37: •Revenue is expected to be $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%. NVIDIA is not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in its outlook.
38: •GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins are expected to be between 71.0% and 72.0%.
39: •GAAP and non-GAAP operating expenses are expected to be approximately $11.0 billion and $10.7 billion, respectively.
40: •For the full year fiscal 2027, NVIDIA expects GAAP and non-GAAP tax rates to be between 16.0% and 18.0%, excluding any discrete items and material changes to NVIDIA’s tax environment.
41: Highlights
42: Data Center
43: •Third-quarter revenue was $107.6 billion, up 21% from the previous quarter and up 110% from a year ago.
44: •Ramped production and began shipping NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 — the fastest product ramp in the company’s history — with racks running at partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Nebius, and coming online soon at SpaceXSI.
45: •Expanded the Vera Rubin cloud ecosystem, announcing general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, general availability of Google Cloud’s Vera Rubin-powered A5X instances and the continued buildout of SpaceXSI’s infrastructure.
46: •Announced Vera Rubin open architecture advances to help the industry scale faster, and revealed that Cisco, Google, Meta, Microsoft and Visionbay are joining many technology leaders advancing infrastructure for Vera Rubin.
47: •Revealed that leading AI natives, cloud providers and neoclouds, including CoreWeave, Meta, Nebius, Nscale, OpenAI and Verda, are building with NVIDIA Vera CPUs to support the growing computing needs of businesses and developers, joining AWS, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and SpaceXSI.
48: •Expanded Anthropic’s access to NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers, and continued to collaborate on design and engineering to optimize future NVIDIA architectures for Anthropic’s workloads.
49: •Announced the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack-scale platform for high-performance computing — combining NVIDIA’s first fully custom data center CPU with the gold standard for HPC networking to drive extreme efficiency and throughput for scientific modeling, simulation and agentic science.
50: •Introduced NVIDIA Rubin HPC, a new GPU in the Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows.
51: •Expanded collaboration with Meta on AI agent Muse and its family of models, with Meta planning expanded deployment of Vera Rubin, Vera CPUs, NVIDIA Spectrum-X™ networking and BlueField®-4 to scale training, inference and agents.
52: •Introduced DSX POD, a reference design for complete Vera Rubin AI factories built by partners inside modular containers, integrated and validated before delivery to accelerate infrastructure deployment.
53: •Announced European ecosystem adoption of NVIDIA DSX™ to reduce AI factory power requirements and enable near-zero facility cooling water consumption.
54: •Announced that NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training and Endpoints benchmark, and Vera Rubin NVL72 demonstrated leading inference performance in its MLPerf Inference preview debut.
55: •Launched NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform and introduced the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture, combining open source OpenShell software, Vera Rubin for model inference, Vera CPUs for agent execution and BlueField®-4 DPUs running NVIDIA Sentry to independently monitor agent behavior and enforce security policies in silicon.
56: •Announced an agreement to acquire Hugging Face to scale its platform and make intelligence more open, capable and accessible.
57: •Announced plans with global supply chain partners, including Amkor Technology, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Siliconware Precision Industries and Unimicron Technology Corporation, to scale critical manufacturing capabilities to meet demand for NVIDIA infrastructure.
58: •Deepened partnership with MediaTek across cloud infrastructure, local computing and automotive, extending NVIDIA’s rack-scale platform to custom XPUs through NVIDIA NVLink Fusion™.
59: •Announced plans with Cisco for USFP, a new optical-module form factor designed to increase bandwidth density and power efficiency for next-generation AI factory networks.
60: •Announced collaboration with Australia’s data center ecosystem on infrastructure supporting a planned buildout of up to 2 gigawatts by 2027 for NVIDIA DSX AI factories.
61: •Introduced NVIDIA Nemotron for Science to help researchers build specialized agents for scientific discovery, and collaborated with global healthcare and life sciences organizations to advance protein design, accelerate drug discovery and expand precision patient care.
62: •Partnered with Palantir to bring sovereign AI intelligence and NVIDIA Nemotron™ open models to critical supply chains.
63: •Partnered with Firebird to scale the company’s total potential AI infrastructure capacity.
64: •Expanded the open source NVIDIA CUDA-Q™ platform with CUDA-Q Logical for fault-tolerant quantum computing development, and ran a record simulation of a fault-tolerant quantum processor on JUPITER at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre.
65: Edge Computing
66: •Third-quarter Edge Computing revenue was $8.2 billion, up 14% from the previous quarter and up 42% from a year ago.
67: •Reinvented Windows PCs with NVIDIA RTX Spark™ laptops, now shipping from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft Surface and MSI.
68: •Launched NVIDIA DLSS 5 in NBA 2K27 and Hogwarts Legacy, bringing AI-powered, photorealistic lighting and materials to GeForce RTX 50 Series GPUs, GeForce NOW and RTX Spark, and coming soon to Where Winds Meet.
69: •Expanded the NVIDIA local AI lineup with a new NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB model, bringing near-frontier AI capabilities to desktops at a more accessible price point, and accelerated leading AI models from NVIDIA Nemotron, Black Forest Labs, Liquid AI and Qwen for running AI agents locally, with expanded support for Hermes, OpenClaw and Perplexity.
70: •Introduced new NVIDIA Alpamayo™ development tools and the NVIDIA Halos™ SAFE framework to help developers build and evaluate autonomous-driving systems.
71: •Expanded partnerships with Mercedes-Benz and Volvo Cars to advance safe automated driving.
72: •Announced European mobility leaders — including Bolt with Lucid, Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles and Einride — are showcasing NVIDIA Hyperion™ use cases for automated vehicles and future robotaxi fleets.
73: •Advanced the NVIDIA Isaac™ robotics platform with new development tools, datasets and runtime, alongside Agile Robots’ introduction of a reference humanoid powered by NVIDIA Jetson Thor™ and built on Isaac GR00T.
74: •Expanded NVIDIA Cosmos™ with tools to train, evaluate and deploy world models for robotics, autonomous vehicles and industrial applications.
75: •Advanced AI-RAN with Nokia and global telecom operators, including T-Mobile’s first AI-RAN call on a commercial network, bringing NVIDIA accelerated computing deeper into wireless networks.

77: Commentary on the quarter by Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s interim CEO and executive vice president and chief financial officer, is available at https://investor.nvidia.com.
78: Conference Call and Webcast Information
79: NVIDIA will conduct a conference call with analysts and investors to discuss its third quarter fiscal 2027 financial results and current financial prospects today at 2 p.m. Pacific time (5 p.m. Eastern time). A live webcast (listen-only mode) of the conference call will be accessible at NVIDIA’s investor relations website, https://investor.nvidia.com. 80: Non-GAAP Measures
81: To supplement NVIDIA’s condensed consolidated financial statements presented in accordance with GAAP, the company uses non-GAAP measures of certain components of financial performance.
82: These non-GAAP measures include non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP gross margin, non-GAAP operating expenses, non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP other income (expense), net, non-GAAP net income, non-GAAP net income, or earnings, per diluted share, and free cash flow. For NVIDIA’s investors to be better able to compare its current results with those of previous periods, the company has shown a reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP financial measures. These reconciliations adjust the related GAAP financial measures to exclude acquisition-related and other costs, other, legal settlement costs, gains/losses from equity securities, net, certain other income and expense, and the associated tax impact of these items where applicable. Beginning in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, NVIDIA’s non-GAAP financial measures no longer exclude stock-based compensation expense. The historical non-GAAP financial information presented has been updated to include stock-based compensation expense. Free cash flow is calculated as GAAP net cash provided by operating activities less both purchases related to property and equipment and intangible assets and principal payments on property and equipment and intangible assets. NVIDIA believes the presentation of its non-GAAP financial measures enhances the users’ overall understanding of the company’s historical financial performance. The presentation of the company’s non-GAAP financial measures is not meant to be considered in isolation or as a substitute for the company’s financial results prepared in accordance with GAAP, and the company’s non-GAAP measures may be different from non-GAAP measures used by other companies.

152: The GPU was initially used to simulate human imagination, enabling the virtual worlds of video games and films. Today, it also simulates human intelligence, enabling a deeper understanding of language, science, and the physical world. Its parallel processing capabilities, supported by tens of thousands of computing cores, are essential for deep learning algorithms. This form of AI, in which software writes itself by learning from large amounts of data, can serve as the brain of computers, robots, and self-driving cars that can perceive, understand and reason about the world. GPU-powered AI solutions are being developed by thousands of enterprises to deliver services and products that would have been immensely difficult or even impossible with traditional coding. Examples include generative AI, which can create new content such as text, code, images, audio, video, molecule structures, and recommendation systems; and agentic AI where systems of AI models work in concert to automatically complete a task.
153: NVIDIA has a platform strategy, bringing together hardware, systems, software, algorithms, libraries, AI models and training data sets, and services to create unique value for the markets we serve. While the computing requirements of these end markets are diverse, we address them with a unified underlying programmable architecture allowing us to support several multi-billion-dollar end markets with the same underlying technology by using a variety of software stacks developed either internally or by third-party developers and partners. The large and growing number of developers and installed base across our platforms strengthens our ecosystem and increases the value of our platform for our customers.
154: Innovation is at our core. We have invested over $76.7 billion in research and development since our inception, yielding inventions that are essential to modern computing. Our invention of the GPU in 1999 sparked the growth of the PC gaming market and redefined computer graphics. With our introduction of CUDA in 2006, we opened the parallel processing capabilities of our GPU to a broad range of compute-intensive applications, paving the way for the emergence of modern AI. In 2012, the AlexNet neural network, trained on NVIDIA GPUs, won the ImageNet computer image recognition competition, marking the “Big Bang” moment of AI. We introduced our first Tensor Core GPU in 2017, built from the ground-up for the new era of AI, and our first autonomous driving system-on-chips, or SoC, in 2018. Our acquisition of Mellanox in 2020 expanded our offerings to include networking, enabled our platforms to be data center scale, and led to the introduction of a new processor class – the data processing unit, or DPU. Over the past 5 years, we have built full software stacks that run on top of our GPUs and CUDA to bring AI to the world’s largest industries, including NVIDIA DRIVE stack for autonomous driving, Clara for healthcare, Omniverse for physical AI applications, and NVIDIA AI Enterprise software – essentially an operating system for enterprise AI applications. In 2023, we introduced our first data center CPU, Grace, built for giant-scale AI and high-performance computing, or HPC. In 2024, we launched the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture – connecting 36 Grace CPUs and 72 Blackwell GPUs in a data center scale, liquid-cooled design – for real-time trillion-parameter inference and training. In fiscal year 2026, we launched and scaled the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra platform, optimized for agentic, reasoning, and physical AI. Building on the architectural breakthroughs of Blackwell and leveraging Dynamo inference software, it delivers a significant increase in token throughput and reduction in cost per token compared to the Hopper generation. More recently, in support of market development, we have accelerated the release cadence of our open AI model platforms including NVIDIA Nemotron for agentic AI and Cosmos for physical AI. With a strong engineering culture, we drive fast, yet harmonized, product and technology innovations in all dimensions of computing including silicon, systems, networking, software and algorithms. More than half of our engineers work on software.

Our AV solution also includes the GPU-based hardware required to train the neural networks before their in-vehicle deployment, as well as to re-simulate their operation prior to any over-the-air software updates. 214: We utilize a fabless and contracting manufacturing strategy, whereby we employ and partner with key suppliers for all phases of the manufacturing process, including wafer fabrication, assembly, testing, and packaging. Additionally, we can avoid many of the significant costs and risks associated with owning and operating manufacturing operations. While we may directly procure certain raw materials used in the production of our products, such as memory, substrates, and a variety of components, our suppliers are responsible for procurement of most raw materials used in the production of our products.
